label: S. 4012

latest_action.text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.

selection.reason: Impact scored and summarised by Gemini.

summary: The Fiscal Commission Act establishes a temporary, bipartisan commission in Congress tasked with addressing the long-term fiscal condition of the Federal Government. The 16-member commission is charged with identifying policies to reduce the debt and deficit, achieving a public debt-to-GDP ratio of not more than 100 percent by fiscal year 2039, improving the solvency of Federal trust funds for at least 75 years, and educating the public about the nation's fiscal state. If the commission approves a report and legislative language by a majority vote—including specific support from members of both major political parties—the resulting bill receives expedited consideration procedures in both the House and the Senate without being subject to amendments.

affected_groups.effect: Selected lawmakers serve on the Fiscal Commission, participate in hearings, vote on recommendations, and handle expedited legislation under special rules.
Required to provide technical assistance, consultations, and testimony to the commission upon request.
affected_groups.group: Federal Agencies and Executive Branch Officials

affected_groups.effect: Subject to a national public awareness and education campaign regarding the nation's fiscal condition and long-term debt risks.

key_provisions: Establishes a 16-member Fiscal Commission composed of Members of Congress and non-governmental outside experts appointed by congressional leadership.

Sets goals for the commission to propose policies that reduce the debt and deficit, achieve a public debt-to-GDP ratio of 100 percent or less by fiscal year 2039, and ensure trust fund solvency for at least 75 years.
Requires the commission to hold at least six public hearings, including field hearings and sessions with executive branch officials and members of Congress.

Mandates that any final report and legislative proposal must be approved by a majority of voting members, which must include at least two votes from Republican-appointed members and at least two votes from Democratic-appointed members.
Requires the Congressional Budget Office to provide estimates and long-term fiscal outlook information at least 48 hours before any vote on the commission's report or recommendations.
Provides a national public awareness campaign completed within 30 days of submitting the commission's report.

Establishes expedited legislative procedures in Congress that allow an implementing bill submitted by the commission to be considered without facing committee delays, amendments, or typical filibuster rules in the Senate.

Exact funding amounts or specific accounts within the Senate budget that will finance the commission's operations.

summary_detail.plain_summary: The Fiscal Commission Act establishes a temporary, bipartisan commission in Congress tasked with addressing the long-term fiscal condition of the Federal Government. The 16-member commission is charged with identifying policies to reduce the debt and deficit, achieving a public debt-to-GDP ratio of not more than 100 percent by fiscal year 2039, improving the solvency of Federal trust funds for at least 75 years, and educating the public about the nation's fiscal state. If the commission approves a report and legislative language by a majority vote—including specific support from members of both major political parties—the resulting bill receives expedited consideration procedures in both the House and the Senate without being subject to amendments.
summary_detail.significance: The Fiscal Commission Act initiates a formal, structured legislative process aimed at confronting federal debt and trust fund solvency through a bipartisan commission with special fast-track voting privileges in Congress. The significance is evaluated as moderate because it establishes a temporary advisory and legislative-drafting body with expedited congressional rules, but any ultimate change to federal spending, revenues, or debt relies entirely on whether the commission reaches consensus and whether Congress subsequently passes the resulting bill.
